question: What do endocrine glands release straight into the bloodstream?
explanation: Spot on! Endocrine glands don't use ducts; they release hormones straight into our blood to act as chemical messengers all over the body. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why can taking a health history for hormone problems be tricky for a nurse?

options.A: Symptoms are usually vague and overlap across different disorders
options.B: Patients almost never remember when their symptoms started
options.C: Endocrine problems only affect one specific body system at a time
options.D: Laboratory tests are completely useless without a physical exam

explanation: You got it! Hormonal issues often start with everyday complaints like constant tiredness, making it hard to pin down the exact cause without patient probing. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which group of people is most likely to experience thyroid disorders?

options.B: Living in a rural farming community
options.D: Being over the age of seventy

explanation: That's correct! Women are diagnosed with thyroid issues much more often than men, so keep a close eye out during assessments. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why is noting a patient's biological sex important when taking an endocrine history?

options.A: It helps identify conditions like thyroid disorders that affect women more often
options.B: It dictates the exact calorie count the patient needs daily
options.C: It replaces the need to perform a complete review of systems
options.D: It proves whether the patient has a genetic metabolic disease

explanation: Well done! Knowing biological sex helps us suspect certain gender-linked conditions, like thyroid imbalances, right from the start. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h2)

question: What are the classic early signs someone might show when developing new type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Painful joints in the hands and feet
options.B: Sudden swelling in both lower legs
options.D: Yellow discoloration of the skin and eyes

explanation: Spot on! When blood sugar is too high, the body pulls water into the urine to flush it out, leaving the patient super thirsty and running to the toilet constantly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why does a nurse need to ask when a patient's symptoms first started?

options.A: Chronic symptoms never require medical treatment
options.B: Rapid onset points to acute problems, while slow onset suggests chronic imbalances
options.C: Insurance companies require exact dates before approving lab tests
options.D: It helps the patient remember to take their medication on time

explanation: Exactly! The timeline helps you figure out if this is a sudden emergency or a long-standing, slow-burning hormonal issue. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which symptom is a classic sign of an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)?
explanation: You nailed it! When the metabolism slows down due to low thyroid hormone, patients feel chilly even when everyone else is warm. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h4)

question: A patient complains of putting on weight fast, being constipated, and feeling cold all the time. Which body system is likely acting up?
explanation: Correct! These are textbook signs of a sluggish metabolism, which points straight to the endocrine system—specifically an underactive thyroid. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why is it important to ask if a patient has ever had surgery on their neck?

options.A: It can damage the thyroid or parathyroid glands
options.B: It stops the pancreas from producing insulin
options.C: It leads to chronic respiratory infections
options.D: It always causes permanent high blood pressure

explanation: Spot on! Because the thyroid and parathyroid glands live right in the neck, past surgeries there can sometimes accidentally disrupt hormone control. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why do nurses always ask about a family history of autoimmune diseases?

options.A: Family history determines the exact medication dose a patient needs
options.B: It is only used to fill out mandatory hospital paperwork
options.C: Genetics prevent patients from ever developing metabolic syndrome
options.D: Autoimmune conditions often cluster together in families, increasing endocrine risks

explanation: That's right! Autoimmune troubles like to run in families, putting patients at a higher risk for conditions like type 1 diabetes or thyroid disease. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which common class of medications is known to raise blood sugar levels over time?
explanation: You got it! Steroids push the liver to make more sugar and make the body less sensitive to insulin, which sends blood glucose climbing. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h6)

question: An asthma patient taking steroid medications suddenly has high blood sugar readings. What should you suspect?

options.A: Severe dehydration from lack of water intake
options.C: A primary failure of the pancreas to produce insulin
options.D: An allergic reaction to the asthma medication

explanation: Spot on! Steroid therapy frequently messes with normal blood sugar control, even in people who have never had diabetes before. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h6)

question: Which hormone does the body pump out in large amounts during long periods of stress?
explanation: That's correct! Cortisol is our main stress hormone. It helps us deal with short-term stress, but high levels over time can cause real metabolic trouble. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why is checking a patient's daily stress level so important when managing diabetes?

options.A: Stress completely cures low blood sugar episodes
options.B: Stress hormones can raise blood sugar levels and make control harder
options.C: Patients with stress never need to take their medications
options.D: Emotional stress is the only cause of metabolic diseases

explanation: Well done! Stress triggers hormones that drive blood sugar up, making it much harder for the patient to keep their levels steady. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h7)
